title: The Harriet Tubman Story
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant profile Harriet Tubman for Black History Month. They cover her birth and childhood in Dorchester County, Maryland, the head injury that left her with sleep disorders, her 1849 escape to Pennsylvania, her roughly thirteen trips back to rescue family and other enslaved people, the Underground Railroad and its coded songs, the 1850 Fugitive Slave Act, the 1860 Troy, New York rescue of Charles Nalle, her Civil War service as a scout and spy and the Combahee River raid, her long fight for a federal pension, her later life in Auburn, New York, her death in 1913, and the proposal to put her on the twenty dollar bill. The episode ends with a Kiva team shout-out and listener contact information.

segments.title: Tour dates and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh lists upcoming tour dates and cities, then the hosts introduce the Harriet Tubman episode for Black History Month and discuss what they learned about her life.

segments.title: Birth, childhood and early enslavement
segments.summary: The hosts discuss uncertain birth year, her Dorchester County, Maryland birth as Araminta Ross, her grandmother Modesty's origins, Athol Pattison's unenforced manumission will, and her work as a child baby-minder and hired-out laborer.

segments.title: Head injury and sleep disorder
segments.summary: As a teenager Tubman was struck in the head by an overseer's iron weight while trying to help a fugitive slave. The injury later was linked to narcolepsy and sleep episodes, which she attributed to religious dreams. Her overseers were unsympathetic.

segments.title: Marriage and escape in 1849
segments.summary: Tubman married John Tubman in 1844 and took the name Harriet from her mother. She escaped in 1849 with her brothers, who turned back, then left alone and reached Pennsylvania, which she likened to heaven. She left family behind and resolved to rescue them.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before the Underground Railroad discussion.

segments.title: Trips back south and the Underground Railroad
segments.summary: Tubman worked as a paid housekeeper and cook in Philadelphia, saving money for trips into Maryland. The hosts describe the Underground Railroad's varied routes, coded songs such as Canaan, timing of escapes, her pistol, the roughly thirteen trips, and the reward on her head.

segments.title: Fugitive Slave Act, Troy rescue and final trips
segments.summary: The 1850 Fugitive Slave Act raised risks for helpers and pushed the Underground Railroad north. In 1860 Tubman helped free Charles Nalle in Troy, New York. Her last trips included rescuing her parents and a family, and she bought land in Auburn, New York from William Seward.

segments.title: Civil War service, pension fight and later life
segments.summary: Tubman served as a Union scout and spy in South Carolina, working with African American troops and leading the Combahee River raid. Her pension claims were denied for decades; she eventually received a widow's pension and later a nurse's pension. She ran a home for elderly African American people, died in 1913, and was proposed for the twenty dollar bill.

segments.summary: Brief closing remarks and contact information.
